newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coupmaker sees full role for rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coupmaker sees full role for rebels.

text.p: The leader of Sierra Leone's military coup said the army and rebels were fed up with fighting and had joined forces to restore peace to the troubled West African state.
Major Johnny Paul Koromah also said he planned a broad-based government in which Foday Sankoh's Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels, who took up arms in 1991, would play a full part.
But ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, now in neighbouring Guinea, said he was optimistic that his supporters and foreign friends would help to restore him as head of state.
Koromah, speaking to Reuters televion on Friday, said: "They (rebels) are tired of fighting. We too are tired of fighting. We need peace and we want it now and we are going to get peace."
He added: "Our intention is to form a broad based government of national unity fully incorporating the RUF to restore everlasting peace and sanity throughout the country."

The coupmakers say they are committed to the democratic process and want a negotiated settlement. "We want elections but there are problems that we have to solve," Koromah said, adding that this would take at least 18 months.
The coup was the third in five years in Sierra Leone, one of the world's poorest countries despite mineral wealth such as diamonds, and has been widely condemned.
An Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe called for Kabbah's reinstatement and officials in Ghana said West African leaders might hold an emergency meeting in Nigeria next week.

Nigeria, the regional power, already had troops in Sierra Leone under a defence pact and sent in reinforcements as part of West African efforts to restore Kabbah to power, but dissident army officers said they would not allow him to return.
Kabbah told Reuters in Guinea's capital of Conakry that he expected to be back home "pretty soon."
"I know the people of Sierra Leone are solidly behind me... although we clearly need external help to restore and moreover to maintain law and order," he said.
Kabbah, whose 1996 election ended four years of army rule, was pessimistic about prospects for a negotiated solution.

"The coup really was a miscalculation on the part of the soldiers. They thought that bringing in the RUF would bring control and they would become chummy, but they were naive in that respect. Instead the RUF has unleashed a terror that went completely out of control," he said.

The rebels have flooded into Freetown since the coup. Previously they had got no further than the approaches to the capital before being driven back by troops trained and helped by South African mercenaries.
RUF founder Sankoh, who signed a fragile peace with Kabbah in November, is under virtual house arrest in Nigeria.
"I'm getting clear messages from my people in Freetown that they want the Nigerians to do whatever is necessary to drive these men out," Kabbah said.
He rejected Koromah's statement that he had undermined the "honour and dignity" of the armed forces by turning a militia of Kamajor traditional hunters against them and fomenting tribal rivalry.

Koromah opposed any foreign intervention. "This is a domestic matter," he said. All the parties in Sierra Leone including politicians, servicemen and people, he said, should "sit together and decide the type of Sierra Leone we want for the 21st century."
